snip.t: Angina, syncope and heart failure are the classic triad of symptomatic aortic stenosis, with a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and a murmur radiating to the carotids.
Medications: Medications are not effective in reversing aortic stenosis, but they can help manage symptoms and associated conditions.
Aortic stenosis: Ejection systolic, right 2nd intercostal space — Radiates to the carotids; slow-rising pulse

Other causes: degenerative calcific aortic stenosis (older patients), a bicuspid aortic valve, infective endocarditis, mitral valve prolapse, and ischaemia (papillary muscle rupture after a heart attack).

qs.q: What are the cardinal symptoms classically associated with significant aortic stenosis?
o: Angina, breathlessness, and syncope
Ascites, jaundice, and peripheral edema
Orthopnea, nocturnal cough, and hemoptysis
Palpitations, claudication, and fever
qs.e: The cardinal symptoms of aortic stenosis are angina, breathlessness, and syncope due to outflow obstruction and myocardial ischemia. Ascites and jaundice are signs of right heart failure or liver pathology.

qs.q: Which pulse characteristic is expected during the physical examination of a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
o: Pulsus parvus et tardus with a slow-rising carotid pulse
Bounding and water-hammer peripheral arterial pulses
An irregularly irregular pulse rhythm without waves
Bisferiens pulse exhibiting two distinct systolic peaks
qs.e: Aortic stenosis causes a delayed or weakened arterial pulse known as pulsus parvus et tardus, characterized by a slow-rising carotid pulse. Bounding pulses are more typical of aortic regurgitation.

qs.q: Where is the murmur of aortic stenosis typically best heard and where does it radiate?
o: Right 2nd intercostal space radiating to the carotid arteries
Apex of the heart radiating strictly into the left axilla
Left lower sternal border increasing with deep inspiration
Third left intercostal space radiating to the epigastrium
qs.e: Aortic stenosis presents with an ejection systolic murmur heard best at the right 2nd intercostal space that radiates to the carotid arteries. Radiating to the axilla is characteristic of mitral regurgitation.

qs.q: What electrocardiographic finding is commonly seen in patients with chronic aortic stenosis reflecting left ventricular adaptation?
o: Left ventricular hypertrophy with ST depression and T wave inversion
Delta waves with shortened PR intervals indicative of pre-excitation
Low voltage QRS complexes throughout all standard limb leads
Right axis deviation and tall R waves in lead V1
qs.e: Aortic stenosis causes left ventricular hypertrophy, which often manifests on ECG as left ventricular hypertrophy alongside ST segment depression and T wave inversion in leads I and aVL. Right axis deviation points toward right heart strain.

qs.q: Which of the following auscultatory findings is classically linked to aortic stenosis?
o: A harsh decrescendo or crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
An opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble
A holosystolic murmur with an S3 gallop
An Austin Flint murmur
qs.e: Aortic stenosis presents with a harsh decrescendo or crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur and can be caused by calcification and degeneration in the elderly. An Austin Flint murmur is associated with aortic regurgitation.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Aortic stenosis is a progressive narrowing of the aortic valve that limits blood flow from the left ventricle, causing symptoms of angina, syncope, and heart failure. It is most common in the elderly due to calcific degeneration, but can also arise from bicuspid valves or rheumatic disease.

sections.p: Aortic stenosis (AS) is defined by a valve area <1.0 cm² or a mean gradient >40 mmHg on echocardiography. The classic murmur is a harsh systolic ejection sound at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
b: Valve area <1.0 cm² or mean gradient >40 mmHg

t.b: Measures valve area, gradients, and ventricular function; confirms AS severity.
Shows left ventricular hypertrophy and aortic root enlargement; suggests chronic pressure overload.
Detects LV hypertrophy, conduction delays, and arrhythmias that may accompany AS.

sections.p: Severity is staged by valve area and mean gradient: mild (1.0–1.5 cm², 20–39 mmHg), moderate (0.75–1.0 cm², 40–59 mmHg), severe (<0.75 cm², ≥60 mmHg).
In developed settings, age‑related calcific degeneration is first. In younger patients, bicuspid aortic valve is common. Rheumatic fever remains a major cause in low‑resource areas.

Patients often report exertional chest pain, fainting spells, and shortness of breath. Physical exam reveals a crescendo‑decrescendo systolic murmur, a delayed carotid upstroke, and a narrow pulse pressure.
Echocardiography is the gold standard. When unavailable, a focused cardiac exam and ECG can suggest AS, but confirmatory imaging is essential.

t.b: Quantifies valve area, gradients, and LV function; defines severity.
Provides detailed valve morphology when echo is suboptimal.
Assesses aortic valve calcification burden; useful when echo is equivocal.

sections.p: Uncontrolled hypertension, new arrhythmias, or worsening dyspnea signal impending heart failure or sudden death. Syncope, especially on exertion, is an urgent red flag.

Treat reversible causes first. Long‑term, beta‑blockers or calcium‑channel blockers relieve angina but avoid excessive vasodilation. Definitive therapy is valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter).
b: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for high‑risk patients

sections.p: Regular echocardiographic surveillance every 1–2 years in asymptomatic severe AS. Prevent rheumatic fever with prompt streptococcal treatment and secondary prophylaxis.
b: Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection risk

sections.p: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension can mimic AS symptoms but have different murmurs and hemodynamics.
b: Pulmonary hypertension – right‑sided murmur, elevated JVP

sections.p: A normal ECG does not exclude AS; LV hypertrophy may be subtle. A low‑grade murmur can be missed in early disease. Echo may underestimate severity if loading conditions are altered.

faq.q: What is the classic murmur of aortic stenosis?
faq.a: A harsh crescendo‑decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
Yes, many patients remain asymptomatic until severe, but they may still have a murmur and LV hypertrophy.

faq.q: Why is beta‑blocker therapy used in AS?
faq.a: It reduces heart rate, prolongs diastole, and improves coronary perfusion, relieving angina without causing severe hypotension.
